title: Speiz — Commercial Real Estate Platform
headline: Making warehouse search faster and more transparent in a fragmented B2B market
intro: Speiz is a commercial real estate platform that helps businesses discover, evaluate, and connect with warehouse spaces across Norway.
The product brings fragmented market information into one experience and helps tenants move from an initial space requirement to a shortlist of relevant options.
I worked across the core tenant experience, combining product design with product-management responsibilities — from research and product requirements to UX/UI, delivery, and iteration.

sections.label: ROLE & SCOPE
sections.headline: Working across design, product, and delivery
paragraphs: My responsibility extended beyond designing individual screens.
I owned major parts of the tenant experience — from understanding user problems and defining product flows to interaction design, detailed UI, and iteration.

As the product evolved, I also took on product-management responsibilities: translating business needs into requirements, helping shape priorities, working closely with developers through delivery, and collaborating with business development and other stakeholders on product decisions.

This meant looking at design decisions not only through the lens of usability, but also through business value, implementation constraints, market realities, and how individual features affected the broader product experience.

sections.label: PROBLEM
sections.headline: Warehouse search was fragmented long before it reached the interface
paragraphs: Finding a warehouse often meant piecing together information from multiple listing platforms, PDFs, brokers, and direct conversations with landlords.

Our early research surfaced recurring problems across the journey: warehouse supply was fragmented, availability was often unclear, important specifications were missing, imagery could be outdated, and tenants relied heavily on PDFs and broker-led email conversations just to understand whether a space was worth considering.
The challenge therefore wasn't simply to create a better property listing interface.
It was to help tenants get from a business requirement to a viable and trustworthy shortlist without spending days gathering and verifying information.

sections.label: RESEARCH & INSIGHTS
sections.headline: The real bottleneck wasn't finding listings — it was knowing which ones were worth pursuing
paragraphs: We combined competitor benchmarking with tenant interviews and conversations with landlords to understand where the existing warehouse-search experience was breaking down.
The competitor audit covered five major Norwegian commercial real estate platforms and helped us understand what the market already supported — and where important gaps remained.

Across the research, one pattern became especially important: access to listings alone wasn't enough. Tenants still had to spend significant effort qualifying each option before they could decide whether it deserved further attention.
That shifted our focus from simply increasing the number of spaces users could browse to improving the quality of the decision journey around them.

items.title: 01 — Coverage matters
items.text: Users need access to enough of the market before search becomes genuinely useful.

items.title: 02 — Information quality matters
items.text: A listing has limited value when specifications, availability, pricing, or imagery are incomplete.

items.title: 03 — Guidance matters
items.text: Different tenants may need different levels of support when turning a requirement into a viable shortlist.

sections.label: DESIGN PROCESS
sections.headline: Turning a fragmented search journey into a coherent product flow
paragraphs: Research gave us the problems to solve, but the next challenge was turning them into a product structure that could support discovery, evaluation, and decision-making without overwhelming the user.
I mapped the core tenant journey, reorganized the information architecture, explored the main flows through wireframes, and progressively moved the experience toward a more guided model.
The key shift was from thinking about Speiz as a collection of property listings to designing an end-to-end journey:

blocks.change: From a collection of property listings to an end-to-end journey: Need → Discover → Shortlist → Evaluate → Decide → Connect.

children.label: SEARCH & DISCOVERY
children.headline: Giving users direct control when they already know what they need
paragraphs: For tenants with clear requirements, Classic Search provided direct access to the market through structured filters, property cards, and a map.
Users could narrow the results by criteria such as location, area, property type, and size, then browse the market independently.
The interface was designed to keep filtering, spatial context, and property information visible together so users could quickly understand both what was available and where.

annotations.text: Refine the market using known requirements.

annotations.title: COMPARABLE PROPERTY CARDS

children.label: SPEIZ PICKS
children.headline: Adding human expertise when search alone wasn't enough
paragraphs: Not every tenant wanted to search the entire market independently.
Speiz Picks introduced a more guided experience where the Speiz team reviewed a tenant's requirements, searched the market, and manually curated spaces specifically for that request.

The product made this human service visible and actionable rather than leaving it buried in emails. Users could understand how the process worked, review their curated shortlist, and give feedback on individual recommendations.

children.label: AI MATCHES
children.headline: Turning a natural-language brief into explainable recommendations
paragraphs: AI Matches introduced a third way to discover warehouse options.

Instead of translating every requirement into a set of filters, tenants could describe what they needed in natural language — for example size, location, loading access, office requirements, move-in timing, or operational constraints.
The system then returned a ranked shortlist of relevant spaces together with additional context explaining how each option matched the request.
This made AI useful not simply as another search interface, but as a way to help users translate an operational need into options they could evaluate.

blocks.headline: Making AI useful meant making it understandable
paragraphs: Commercial real estate decisions involve significant cost, operational constraints, and long-term commitments. Simply presenting an AI-generated shortlist would not be enough.
We therefore designed AI Matches as a decision-support experience rather than a black-box recommendation engine.
Recommendations included match signals, explanations, supporting sources, and a summary of where an option worked well — or where it did not fully meet the brief.
Users could then accept the direction, request more options, or refine the original criteria.
The goal was not to replace tenant judgment. It was to reduce the work required to reach a shortlist worth investigating.

children.label: SPACE DETAILS
children.headline: Making warehouse options easier to evaluate without relying on PDFs
paragraphs: Discovery was only useful if tenants could understand what they had found.
A promising warehouse still needed to be evaluated against operational requirements: size, location, availability, facilities, pricing, imagery, and other specifications.
We therefore focused on bringing the information needed for early evaluation into a structured property experience rather than forcing users to move between listings, PDFs, and broker communication.

blocks.title: A closer look at the space

children.label: DECISION ACTIONS
children.headline: Turning browsing into an active decision process
paragraphs: A marketplace can easily become an endless browsing experience.
We wanted each recommendation to help the tenant move closer to a decision.

Across the product, users could react to spaces rather than simply open and close listings. Curated recommendations could be accepted or rejected, while the broader experience supported lightweight interest and connection states.
These actions created clearer signals for both the tenant and the Speiz team, helping the product identify which options were worth pursuing and which should be removed from consideration.

sections.label: IMPACT
sections.headline: What changed
paragraphs: The tenant experience evolved from a conventional property-search model into a product with multiple layers of discovery and guidance.

Users could explore the market independently through Classic Search, receive human-curated options through Speiz Picks, or use AI Matches to turn a natural-language requirement into an explained shortlist.

Structured property information and explicit decision actions then helped users move from discovery toward evaluation and follow-up without relying on the disconnected workflows Speiz was created to replace.
All three discovery approaches described above were implemented as part of the product rather than remaining conceptual directions.

sections.label: LEARNINGS
sections.headline: Better search was not enough
paragraphs: One of the biggest lessons from Speiz was that access to more listings does not automatically create a better decision experience.
The harder problem was creating confidence: Are these options relevant? Is the underlying information reliable? Why is this space being recommended? What should I do next?

As the product evolved, my own role evolved with it. Working across product requirements, design, stakeholders, and delivery pushed me to think less in terms of individual screens and more in terms of interconnected product systems.

If I continued evolving Speiz today, I would keep focusing on transparency — particularly around recommendation quality, data freshness, and making the reasoning behind suggested spaces even easier to understand.
